topics.title: What is C Language?
topics.content: C is a high-level, general-purpose programming language developed by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs in the early 1970s. It is known for its efficiency, performance, and close relationship with hardware, often referred to as a 'middle-level' language. C provides constructs that map efficiently to typical machine instructions, making it ideal for system programming.
key_points: High-level, general-purpose programming language
Developed by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs in early 1970s
Known for efficiency, performance, and close hardware relationship
Often called a 'middle-level' language
Constructs map efficiently to machine instructions
Ideal for system programming

subtopics.title: Why is C Important?
subtopics.content: C is important because it forms the foundation for many modern programming languages (C++, Java, Python, JavaScript). It is the primary language for writing operating systems, compilers, and embedded systems. C programs execute very fast because they are compiled into machine code, offering fine-grained control over hardware. C programs are also portable — they can be compiled and run on different systems with minimal changes.
key_points: Foundation for C++, Java, Python, JavaScript
Primary language for operating systems, compilers, embedded systems
Programs execute fast — compiled into machine code
Fine-grained control over hardware
Portability — write once, compile anywhere with minimal changes

subtopics.title: C as a Middle-Level Language
subtopics.content: C combines features of both high-level and low-level languages. High-level features include structured programming, functions, and data types. Low-level features include direct memory manipulation via pointers, bitwise operations, and direct access to hardware. This blend makes C powerful and flexible for a wide range of applications.
key_points: Combines high-level and low-level features
High-level: structured programming, functions, data types
Low-level: pointers, bitwise operations, direct hardware access
Powerful and flexible for wide range of applications

topics.title: History of C Language
topics.content: C language evolved through several predecessor languages before being standardized internationally.
key_points: ALGOL (1960) — Early structured programming language by ACM
BCPL (1967) — Developed by Martin Richards for compilers and OS
B Language (1969) — Developed by Ken Thompson at Bell Labs, simplified BCPL without types
C Language (1972) — Developed by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs
Created to rewrite UNIX (originally in assembly and B)
Name 'C' comes from being based on 'B' language
K&R C (1978) — First widely influential C description by Kernighan and Ritchie
ANSI C / C89 (1989) — Standardized by ANSI (X3.159-1989)
ISO C90 (1990) — Adopted by ISO as ISO/IEC 9899:1990
C99, C11, C17 — Continued ISO updates

topics.title: Application Areas of C
topics.content: C is used extensively across many domains in computing.

areas.details: C is the primary language for developing operating systems. Examples include UNIX, Linux kernel, parts of Windows, and macOS kernels. Its low-level capabilities allow direct interaction with hardware components like memory and peripherals.
Used for writing compilers, assemblers, text editors, and interpreters. Example: GCC (GNU Compiler Collection) is largely written in C.

Ideal for programming microcontrollers and embedded systems due to memory efficiency and direct hardware access. Found in washing machines, digital cameras, smart home devices, automotive systems, medical equipment.

Many game engines and high-performance game logic are written in C/C++. C offers the speed and control necessary for complex graphics, physics, and real-time simulations. Example: Unreal Engine uses C++.
Core components of many DBMS are written in C. Examples: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle's internal components often utilize C/C++ for performance-critical operations.
Used to create network device drivers. Tools like ping, ipconfig, netstat are often implemented in C.
Libraries for 2D and 3D graphics (OpenGL, DirectX APIs) are often implemented in C/C++. Used in CAD applications, image processing software, and visual effects.

topics.title: Features of C Language
topics.content: C has several distinguishing features that make it a widely-used and powerful programming language.

features.description: Relatively small set of keywords and straightforward syntax. Programs are fast and efficient because they are compiled directly into machine code. No garbage collection or extensive runtime checks.
Source code can be compiled and run on different hardware platforms and operating systems with minimal or no changes. 'Write once, compile anywhere' through standardized libraries (ANSI/ISO C).

Allows direct memory access through pointers. Pointers are variables that store memory addresses. Provides powerful control over memory for efficient data structures and algorithms. Requires careful handling to avoid memory leaks or segmentation faults.

Standard library provides built-in functions: I/O (printf, scanf), string manipulation (strlen, strcpy), math (sqrt, sin), memory allocation (malloc, free). Users can also create custom functions and libraries.
Promotes modular programming through functions. Complex problems broken into smaller sub-problems. Benefits: code reusability, easier debugging, better organization, improved readability.
'variable', 'Variable', and 'VARIABLE' are three distinct identifiers. Keywords, variable names, and function names must use consistent casing.
Source code must be translated into machine code before execution. A C compiler translates high-level C code into executable binary code. Results in highly optimized and fast-executing programs.

topics.title: Structure of a C Program
topics.content: Every C program follows a standard structure with specific sections.

sections.description: Description of the program, name, creation date/time. Specified at the start in the form of comments. Optional.
Header files included using #include directive. Syntax: #include <filename.h> for standard headers, #include "filename.h" for user-defined headers. Example: #include <stdio.h>
The #define preprocessor creates constants throughout the program. Placed before main(). Written in uppercase. Examples: #define PI 3.14, #define PRINCIPAL 5000.00
Variables and functions declared here can be used anywhere in the program.

main() is the entry point of every C program. Program execution begins and ends within main(). Syntax: int main() { /* code */ return 0; }. Only one main function per program. int main() requires return 0; at end. void main() requires getch(); at end.
User defined functions can be defined and declared here.

key_points: Comments: single-line (//) and multi-line (/* */)
All statements must end with semicolon (;)
Only ONE main() function allowed per program
int main() requires 'return 0;' at end
void main() requires 'getch();' at end

header_files.purpose: String conversion routines, Memory allocation, Random number generator

topics.title: Execution Flow of a C Program
topics.content: A C program goes through several stages from source code to execution.

stages.description: Handles directives like #include (inserts header file content) and #define (macro substitution). Generates an expanded source file (.i).
Translates the preprocessed code into assembly code. Compiler (gcc) checks for syntax errors, type errors, etc.
Converts assembly code into machine-readable object code.
Combines object files with necessary library functions to create an executable file. Linker resolves external references.
The OS loader places the program into memory. CPU starts executing machine instructions from main(). Program terminates when main() returns or exit function is called.

program_development_steps: Requirement Gathering — Define the problem statement and boundaries
Analysis — Understand the problem, gather preliminary requirements, eliminate unimportant aspects
Design — Use algorithms and flowcharts to develop the program design
Coding — Convert algorithm to program using a high-level language
Testing — Test on multiple test cases, verify correctness
Maintenance — Update and correct for changed conditions

topics.title: Input/Output in C
topics.content: C provides standard library functions for I/O operations in <stdio.h>. Two main categories: Character I/O and Formatted I/O.

subtopics.title: Reading a Character: getchar()
subtopics.content: getchar() reads a single character from standard input (keyboard). Returns the character read as an integer (ASCII value) or EOF on failure. Declared in <stdio.h>.

example.output:
Enter a character: A
You entered: A

subtopics.title: Writing a Character: putchar()
subtopics.content: putchar() writes a single character to standard output (screen). Takes an integer argument representing the character (ASCII value). Returns the character written on success, or EOF on error. Declared in <stdio.h>.

subtopics.title: Formatted Input: scanf()
subtopics.content: scanf() reads formatted input from standard input (keyboard). Syntax: int scanf("format string", &variable1, &variable2, ...); The & (address-of operator) is crucial. Returns the number of items successfully read, or EOF on failure. Declared in <stdio.h>.

format_specifiers.purpose: Reads a string (until whitespace, no & needed for arrays)

examples.output:
Enter your age: 30
You are 30 years old.

Enter name and height (e.g., John 1.75): Alice 1.68
Name: Alice, Height: 1.68 meters

subtopics.title: Formatted Output: printf()
subtopics.content: printf() sends formatted output to standard output (screen). Syntax: int printf("format string", argument1, argument2, ...); Returns the number of characters printed, or negative value on error. Declared in <stdio.h>.

format_specifiers.purpose: Prints a floating-point number (default 6 decimal places)
Prints float with N decimal places (e.g., %.2f)

examples.output:
Value (2 decimal places): 123.46
Value (total width 10, 2 dec):     123.46
Count (padded with spaces):     5

topics.title: Summary & Key Takeaways
topics.content: C is a powerful, efficient, and portable middle-level programming language. It forms the backbone of operating systems, embedded systems, and many performance-critical applications. Understanding C's structure (header files, main(), sections) is fundamental. The execution flow involves preprocessing, compilation, assembly, linking, loading, and runtime. Character I/O (getchar(), putchar()) handles single characters. Formatted I/O (scanf(), printf()) allows versatile input/output using format specifiers.
key_points: C — powerful, efficient, portable middle-level language
Backbone of OS, embedded systems, performance-critical apps
Structure: documentation, preprocessor, definition, global declaration, main(), UDF
Execution: preprocessing → compilation → assembly → linking → loading → execution
Character I/O: getchar() reads, putchar() writes single characters
Formatted I/O: scanf() reads, printf() writes using format specifiers
